## Part I
This part uses the **Cereal** dataset in the **Lock5Data** package. Make sure to load the relevant packages.
The plots are shown below. For each one, write R code to reproduce it. Elements such as titles, labels, colors, and themes can differ, but make appropriate modifications instead of relying on defaults. The suggested ggplot theme is provided; you may use another theme. Open **Show solution** to see one possible solution.



Plot 1. (This is not a ggplot; the variable used is **Calories**)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Show solution"}
stem(Cereal$Calories)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

   8 | 074
  10 | 0178347777788
```

::: {.cell}


Plot 3. **theme_classic()**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Show solution"}
Cereal %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=Calories,y=Sugars)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 200,linetype='dashed')
```

## Part II

This part uses the UNICEF Changing Childhood Project data (the same dataset used in [Lecture 5](../lectures/lecture_5/lecture_5.html){target="_blank"}). It's an open-ended exploration of the data, giving you practice handling a complicated dataset with `tidyverse` and generating visualizations with `ggplot2`. Think about what conclusions you can draw from the tables and visualizations, and write code to reproduce them. In addition, try other variables in the data to generate your own visualizations (see if you can find anything interesting!)

I used these variables:

- `COUNTRYNEW`: country
- `AGE`: age group: `1` = 15-19, `2` = 20-24, `3` = 40-44, `4` = 45-49, `5` = 50-54, `6` = 55-59, `7` = 60-64, `8` = 65-69, `9` = 70-74, `10` = 75-99.







### 1. Trust in the police

The table shows the top countries in terms of the percentage of respondents who trust the police "a lot."  The boxplot shows the univariate distribution of this percentage.

- `COUNTRYNEW`: country
- `WP22096`: trust in the country's police to protect the respondent: `1` = a lot, `2` = a little, `3` = not at all, `8` = don't know, `9` = refused.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Show solution"}
df.child %>%
  filter(WP22096 %in% 1:3) %>%
  group_by(COUNTRYNEW) %>%
  summarise(percent1= mean(WP22096 == 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(percent1)) 
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

   COUNTRYNEW     percent1
   <chr>             <dbl>
 1 Morocco           0.669
 2 Zimbabwe          0.638

10 France            0.385
# ℹ 11 more rows
```

:::

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Show solution"}
df.child %>%
  filter(WP22096 %in% 1:3) %>%
  group_by(COUNTRYNEW) %>%
  summarise(percent1= mean(WP22096 == 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = percent1)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  ggtitle("Percentage in a country who trust the police 'a lot'")
```

### 2. Gender equality

Compare responses from selective countries to the questions about technology skills (`WP22078`) and cooking (`WP22079`).

- `WP22078`: whether it is more important for girls, boys, or equally important for both to learn how to use a smartphone, computer, or tablet
- `WP22079`: whether it is more important for girls, boys, or equally important for both to learn how to cook
- Coding: `1` = girls, `2` = boys, `3` = equally important, `8` = don't know, `9` = refused.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Show solution"}
df.child %>%
  filter(COUNTRYNEW %in% c("United States", "Japan", "Nigeria")) %>%
  filter(WP22078 %in% 1:3, WP22079 %in% 1:3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(WP22078), y = as.factor(WP22079))) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~COUNTRYNEW) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "1 = girls, 2 = boys, 3 = equally important",
    x = "Importance to learning technology skills",
    y = "Importance to learning how to cook",
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](homework_5_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


### 3. Generation optimism

Create a new variable by adding up the following. They are all 

- `WP22140`: Age; coded as '1' = 15-24, '2' = 40 or older.
- `WP22118`: whether children's mental well-being is better or worse than in their parents' time; coded as `1` = better, `2` = worse, `3` = the same, `8` = don't know, `9` = refused.`


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Show solution"}
df.child %>%
  filter(WP22118 %in% 1:3, WP22140 %in% 1:2) %>%
  filter(COUNTRYNEW %in% c("United States", "Germany")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(WP22140), fill = as.factor(WP22118))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("1" = "Green", "2" = "Red", "3" = "Grey"),
    labels = c("1" = "Better", "2" = "Worse", "3" = "The same")
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~COUNTRYNEW) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Age group (1 = 15-24, 2 = 40+)",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Children's mental well-being"
  ) +
  ggtitle("Children's mental well-being compared to parents: 1 = better, 2 = worse, 3 = the same")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](homework_5_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
